newsitem.title: USA: Ill. agencies watch possible Tollway ruling impact.
newsitem.headline: Ill. agencies watch possible Tollway ruling impact.

text.p: Officials from three Illinois agency's that issue debt for development, housing and education facilities said Friday they are closely following a court ruling last week negating state tollway budget practices.

While saying they have confidence in their current practices, Illinois Development Finance Authority Director Bobby Wilkerson and Illinois Educational Facilities Authority Executive Director Thomas Conley said attorneys are studying last week's ruling to determine if it could also apply to those agencies.

Robert Kugel, chief financial officer of the Illinois Housing Development Authority, said board members have been monitoring developments in the Cook County case and await a final order before determining whether it would have any impact.

Judge Stephen Schiller ruled last week that the state Toll Highway Authority's practice of making ongoing budget appropriations without oversight of the governor or legislature ran afoul of state constitutional requirements.
Schiller later determined the Toll Authority would have until Dec. 15 to comply with budget requirements or be enjoined from all expenditures excluding debt service payments.

The Toll Authority has approximately $930 million of outstanding debt backed by the tolls it collects from motorists. Chief Legal Counsel George Sotos contended in court that restricting payments to debt service alone could adversely effect bond holders and trustees.
All three agencies have issued far more outstanding debt than the Toll Authority. They receive no state appropriations and their issuances are not legal or moral obligations of the state.
The Development Finance Authority has approximately $5 billion outstanding debt, the Housing Development Authority $2 billion and the Educational Facilities Authority $1.35 billion.
Wilkerson said he discussed the developments with agency counsel Thursday and is watching it closely.
"While we are interested and want to be thoughtful about it, we think we are in good shape," Wilkerson said.
Conley said he did not believe submitting a budget to Gov. Jim Edgar would pose a problem, nor would it influence debt issuance or the ratings of revenue bonds already issued by the authority.
"As a lawyer, his decision makes a good deal of sense, I'm just not sure how it applies to a wide variety of agencies," Conley said.
